sub.en: Compare with Lesson 25. What changes when the situation is imaginary rather than likely?

items.q: If I ___ the world, I would start with clean water.
items.why: The second conditional uses the Past Simple in the if-clause and would in the other half. The past form does not mean past time — it means “this is imaginary”.

items.q: If I ran the world, I ___ start with clean water.
If I ___ you, I’d take the money.
items.why: “If I were you” keeps were. This is the one place English still does it.

items.q: What ___ you do if you had a year off?
If it ___ tomorrow, we’ll stay in. (likely — it often does)
items.why: RECYCLED from Lesson 25: for something likely, the FIRST conditional — present + will.

items.q: If it ___ in the desert, everything would change. (very unlikely)
I ___ live abroad — I’d miss my family too much.
A cure for that disease ___ in 1998.
items.why: RECYCLED from Lesson 29: the passive, because who found it doesn’t matter here.

acts.title: One change each
text: We asked four people the same question: if you could change one thing about the world, what would it be? The answers were less dramatic than we expected.

AN ECONOMIST: “I would make school free everywhere, to eighteen. Not because education solves everything — it doesn’t — but because every other problem gets cheaper to fix if more people can read the argument about it.”

A MARINE BIOLOGIST: “I would cool the sea by one degree. The coral reefs would come back, and about a quarter of all fish species live in them. If the reefs went, we would find out very fast how much we needed them.”

A NURSE: “I would give every country the drugs it already knows how to make. Most people who die of malaria die of something that was cured somewhere else decades ago. It isn’t an invention problem. It’s a delivery problem.”
A TEACHER: “If I ran the world, I would ban meetings before ten. I know that isn’t global hunger. But you asked what I would change, and I answered honestly, which is more than most people do.”

use: Isn’t it rather a crazy idea?
tts: So what did you think about the idea for a pill that would make us super intelligent? — Great idea. I mean, we live in a complicated world and we need all the brain power we can get.

True, but do you think it’s likely that scientists will be able to come up with a super-intelligence drug? Isn’t it rather a crazy idea? — No, not at all. You can already buy drugs to help you to concentrate.
And if such a pill existed, would everybody be able to afford it? — That’s the real question. If only rich people could buy it, it would make the world less fair, not more intelligent.

write.q: Answer the question in 6 sentences: if you could change one thing about the world, what would it be? Use the second conditional four times, one “If I were you” or “If I were…”, and one first conditional about something that really might happen.
write.ph: If I could change one thing…
write.model: If I could change one thing, I would make public transport free in every city over half a million people. If it were free, fewer people would drive, and the air in my city would be measurably better within a year. I wouldn’t make it free everywhere immediately — small towns would need something different. If I were the mayor, I would start with one line and measure it properly. That is the part nobody does. And if the city announces anything this spring, I’ll write to them, because a small real change beats a large imaginary one.

speak.q: Answer out loud: If you could change one thing about the world, what would it be, and why? What would happen if you did? What wouldn’t you change?
speak.model: If I could change one thing, I’d make public transport free. If it were free, fewer people would drive and the air would be better. I wouldn’t change the working week — I think people would just fill it.
